title: Could we publicly disclose exactly how a critical algorithm reaches its decisions, if challenged?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether an organization could withstand a legal disclosure challenge to a critical decision-making algorithm, rather than assuming IP or security claims would protect it indefinitely.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: If challenged in court or by a civil-society organization, could we publicly disclose exactly how a critical eligibility or administrative algorithm reaches its decisions — or are we relying on intellectual-property or security claims that a court, as Spain's Supreme Court did with BOSCO, might reject?
rationale: Civio's seven-year fight over Spain's BOSCO algorithm ended with the Supreme Court holding that IP and generic security claims do not justify withholding an eligibility algorithm's logic from the public — a precedent any organization running a similar algorithm should assume could apply to them.
follow_up_actions: Request the current public algorithm documentation publication record for every eligibility-determining system.
Ask legal whether current non-disclosure justifications would withstand a Civio-style challenge.
Confirm a proactive publication plan exists rather than a defensive one.

citations.title: Civio pulls back the curtain on public algorithms — Spain's Supreme Court orders the Government to release BOSCO's source code
